newsitem.title: USA: Dying man plots his suicide and court fight.
newsitem.headline: Dying man plots his suicide and court fight.

text.p: Noel David Earley spends his days, dying, in an apartment cluttered with medical equipment -- and full of fight.

The 47-year-old's 6-foot frame is being wasted by Lou Gehrig's disease -- amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. ALS is an untreatable, progessive, neuromuscular disease in which the sufferer's muscles atrophy, causing paralysis and eventually death.

But Earley, his legs and left arm paralysed and withered, his weak voice barely audible, refuses to go gently into that good night. Instead, he has chosen to rail against those who would prevent his right and what he says is everyone's right to die.
"I'm not doing this for me. I'm doing this for the hundreds of thousands of others who can't speak for themselves," said the man who has become a spokesman for the right-to-die movement.

Last spring, he testified before the Rhode Island legislature, arguing that a law making assisted suicide a felony punishable by 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine should be struck. But the legislators revived and reinstated the law.
Earley and the American Civil Liberties Union are fighting to have it declared unconstitutional in federal court.
But it is unlikely Earley, who keeps a pine coffin at the foot of his bed, will choose to live long enough to go to trial.
"I'll give a videotaped deposition," he said, shortly after remarking that he will commit suicide when he loses his voice.
When he was diagnosed two years ago, Earley, who holds two college degrees, was the head of a daycare centre in Cambridge, Massachusetts, for victims of Alzheimer's disease.

"There is no pain associated with ALS and my immune system is intact," he said in a raspy whisper as an IV bag filled with his daily supply of nurishment hung above his head. "I can't drink liquids. They go straight into my lungs."
Divorced and childless, for the past three months he has had to depend on friends for survival.

"Someone comes in the morning and gets me out of bed. I sit at the computer and answer the mail. Then I stay here all day," he said, indicating the motorized reclining chair where his thin body lays covered with a bright pink blanket, answering the phone and receiving reporters.
Maintaining his dignity is important to Earley as is not imposing too much on his friends.

He wants the world to witness his ordeal so people will understand his need and possibly that of others for suicide. "My body, my choice. Isn't that what the women's movement says?" he asked rhetorically, adding he has received many calls from people asking him not to commit suicide.
"I must have about 20,000 people around the world praying for me. It doesn't seem to have had any effect ... My personal relationship with my higher power is personal," he said.
Through it all, the Vietnam War veteran is not angry or bitter about his fatal condition, saying, "I've had a full life."

He has talked with Dr. Jack Kevorkian, the top U.S. assisted-suicide activist. "We spoke at length on the phone over the summer and he said when the time came I should come to Michigan ... But I found someone locally who would help me instead. Local is better."

Rhode Island Attorney General Jeff Pine has vowed to prosecute anyone who assists Earley and Earley is very circumspect about saying who gave him a syringe and supplied him with a lethal drug mixture.
"See that big muscle on your thumb. That's all I need to work," he said and then struggled with his lighter as a cigarette dangled from his lips.
"Well, I'm not going to die of lung cancer," he grinned from under a shaggy moustache.
